theme: He raises the poor from the dust, the Magnificat’s psalm
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 113. This is the first psalm in the Hallel (Psalms 113 to 118). It praises the God who raises the poor from the dust, and it echoes Hannah’s song and Mary’s song. Read it beside the Magnificat.
settingTheScene: Psalm 113 opens a group of six psalms sung at Passover and other great feasts. It is short and structured as three stanzas: God’s name is to be praised, God is high above all nations, and yet he stoops to lift the needy. It stands behind Hannah’s song in 1 Samuel 2 and Mary’s song in Luke 1. Reading it just after Luke 1 and 2 shows where Mary found her words.
observation: “Praise the LORD! Praise, O servants of the LORD, praise the name of the LORD!” (v. 1).
“Blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and forevermore!” (v. 2).
“From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the LORD is to be praised!” (v. 3).
“The LORD is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens!” (v. 4).
“Who is like the LORD our God, who is seated on high” (v. 5).
“Who looks far down on the heavens and the earth?” (v. 6).
“He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap” (v. 7).
“He gives the barren woman a home, making her the joyous mother of children” (v. 9).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with praise and its scope grows wider with each verse. First the servants of the LORD, then all time (“from this time forth and forevermore”), then all space (“from the rising of the sun to its setting”). The name of the LORD is to be praised everywhere and always.

Then the question: “Who is like the LORD our God?” He is seated on high, above all nations and above the heavens. In the ancient world, the great gods were high and distant. But here is the surprise. This God “looks far down on the heavens and the earth.” He is so high that even the heavens are far below him, and yet he looks down and sees the lowly.

What does he do? He raises the poor from the dust. He lifts the needy from the ash heap and seats them with princes, even the princes of his people. And he gives the barren woman a home and a family. This is the pattern of the Bible’s story: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and Elizabeth. Again and again the barren woman receives a child, and God’s purposes advance through those who seemed least likely.

Now read Luke 1 again. Mary sings, “He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate.” She draws on this psalm and on Hannah’s song. Elizabeth, barren, has a son in her old age. Mary herself is of humble estate, and she carries the Son of God. The one who raises the poor from the dust has come down in person. The incarnation is the greatest instance of the psalm: the God who is high above all stoops lower than anyone could expect, to a manger and a cross, and lifts people up.
connection: 1 Samuel 2:1-10 is Hannah’s song, and Luke 1:46-55 is Mary’s. Isaiah 57:15 says God dwells in the high and holy place and also with the contrite and lowly. Philippians 2:5-11 describes Christ’s descent and exaltation. Ephesians 2:4-6 says God raised us up with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly places. James 4:6 says God gives grace to the humble. Matthew 26:30 says that after the Last Supper they sang a hymn, likely the Hallel.
application:
Praise God today from the “rising of the sun to its setting.” Make it a thread through your day.

Think of someone overlooked or lowly. Ask how you might lift them up.

Thank God that he lifted you from the dust through Christ.
prayerPrompts: Praise God for raising the poor from the dust.
Tell him what he has lifted you from.
Bless his name now and forevermore.
